newsitem.title: CANADA: Chretien opposes across-the-board Canadian tax cut.
newsitem.headline: Chretien opposes across-the-board Canadian tax cut.

text.p: Prime Minister Jean Chretien has slammed the door on tax relief for all citizens, saying it was not the right thing to do in a society like Canada.

"If ever the government can get hold of some money, there's still some social programs in our society that need to be cured," he told a Liberal fundraiser on Tuesday night as he criticized opposition calls for tax cuts.

"We had to neglect a lot of things in the last few years, and I am not the one who will want to have an across-the-board tax cut for everybody. I don't think it is the right thing to do in a society like Canada."

"It's extremely important for all of us to realize that the most important thing we have to do is not start to spend the money that we have not yet in the bank, and we have to stay the course until we have balanced the books properly," Chretien added.
"And after that, if we have money we'll use it properly. But I don't want to, at this moment, to start to spend the money."
Chretien's finance minister, Paul Martin, last week ruled out a broad-based tax cut for now but allowed for tax reform that would reallocate within the present revenue system.
The three main opposition parties -- the separatist Bloc Quebecois and the Conservative and Reform parties -- have all called for cuts in unemployment insurance premia.

Conservative and Reform members have agitated for income tax cuts as well, and on Thursday Reform leader Preston Manning is unveiling a pre-election campaign package expected to call for specific tax cuts.
Chretien has not called federal elections but is widely expected to do so next year.
"I'm not going to buy votes with the Canadian people in the next election...I will not get involved in a bidding war about so-called promises in the future and not deliver the goods," he said.

And, turning former U.S. President George Bush's ill-fated no-new-tax pledge on its head, he said: "As far as this government is concerned, Canadians don't need to read my lips. They can read our record."
